new_quiz.q: How do you open the console while the game runs in the editor?
choices: Press F9
Press the backtick key, which on most keyboards is the key above Tab
Press Ctrl+B
Press the G key in the viewport
new_quiz.explain: The backtick key opens the console, where you type commands such as stat fps. On most keyboards it is the key above Tab.

new_quiz.q: Which console command hides the stats that are shown on the screen?
choices: stat none
stat off
stat hide
stat unit
new_quiz.explain: The command stat none hides the stats again. The commands stat fps and stat unit turn stats on.

new_quiz.q: What kind of information do the commands stat fps and stat unit show?
choices: The names of the actors in the level
The list of assets that are not saved
The errors in your Blueprints
Performance numbers, such as the frame rate and frame times
new_quiz.explain: These stat commands print performance numbers on the screen. They tell you how fast the game runs without any guessing.

new_quiz.q: What is a show flag?
choices: A marker that you place in the level
A node that writes text on the screen
A switch that turns one kind of visual information on or off
A warning in the Output Log
new_quiz.explain: Show flags are in the Show menu of the viewport. Each one turns one kind of visual information on or off, for example Collision or Bounds.

new_quiz.q: What does the Print String node do?
choices: It writes text on the screen
It saves text to a file on disk
It prints the level on paper
It renames the selected actor
new_quiz.explain: Print String writes a text on the screen while the game runs. It is the simplest way to see that a part of a Blueprint was reached.

new_quiz.q: You run the same Print String node twice with the same Key. What do you see?
choices: Two lines, one under the other
An error message in red
The second message replaces the first one
No message at all
new_quiz.explain: Messages with the same Key share one line on the screen. A new message replaces the old one, which keeps the screen clean when a value updates often.

new_quiz.q: What is the Output Log?
choices: A panel that lists the actors in the level
A file that stores your saved games
A window where the engine and your Blueprints write messages, warnings and errors
A tool that records where the engine spends its time
new_quiz.explain: The Output Log collects text from the engine and from your Blueprints. You open it with Window, then Output Log, and you can filter it to show only warnings and errors.

new_quiz.q: What does a breakpoint on a Blueprint node do?
choices: It deletes the node when the game starts
It makes the game pause when that node runs
It skips the node while the game runs
It prints the name of the node on the screen
new_quiz.explain: A breakpoint pauses the game at the moment the node runs. While it is paused, you can look at the values in the graph.

new_quiz.q: Which key sets a breakpoint on the selected node?
choices: F9
F8
F5
new_quiz.explain: You select a node and press F9 to set a breakpoint on it. The same key removes it again.

new_quiz.q: The game is paused on a breakpoint. What does pressing F10 do?
choices: It stops Play in Editor
It removes all breakpoints
It restarts the level
It steps over one node, so the nodes run one at a time
new_quiz.explain: F10 runs the next node and pauses again. Stepping lets you follow the flow of the graph one node at a time.

new_quiz.q: How do you keep an eye on the value of a pin in the Blueprint Debugger window?
choices: Double-click the pin
Right-click the pin and choose Watch This Value
Drag the pin into the Output Log
Select the pin and press F9
new_quiz.explain: Watch This Value marks the pin as watched. The Blueprint Debugger window then shows its value while the game is paused.

new_quiz.q: You set a breakpoint on the Jump node and press Play, but the game never pauses. What do you check first?
choices: That the Output Log is closed
That the Blueprint is saved in another folder
That you did the action that makes the node run
That the level has a Player Start
new_quiz.explain: A breakpoint only pauses the game when its node runs. If you never jump, the Jump node never runs and nothing pauses.

new_quiz.q: Why is reading the Third Person template a fast way to learn?
choices: It is the only project that can be opened in the editor
It has no Blueprints, so it is simple
It cannot be changed, so nothing can break
It is a working game where you can see how input, movement and the camera are connected
new_quiz.explain: The template already works. Following its graphs shows you how the parts connect, which is faster than writing everything from nothing.

new_quiz.q: What does the GameMode of the template do?
choices: It sets the rules of the game and decides which character the player uses
It draws the level in the viewport
It stores the meshes of the character
It records the input of the player to a file
new_quiz.explain: The GameMode is the Blueprint that holds the rules of the game. One of its settings is which character the player gets.

new_quiz.q: What is an Input Action event in the character Blueprint?
choices: A node that runs once when the game starts
A node that fires when the player presses a key or moves a stick
A node that plays an animation
A node that changes the camera boom
new_quiz.explain: The Input Action event is where the input enters the graph. You follow the chain from this node to the node that moves the character.

new_quiz.q: Where do you see the components that the character is made of?
choices: In the Output Log
In the World Settings
In the Components panel of the Blueprint
In the Place Actors panel
new_quiz.explain: The Components panel lists the parts of the Blueprint, such as the mesh and the camera. Each one has its own job.

new_quiz.q: What is the camera boom of the character?
choices: The sound the camera makes
The arm that holds the camera behind the character
The light that follows the character
The mesh that shows the character
new_quiz.explain: The camera boom is an arm between the character and the camera. Its length decides how far the camera sits behind the character.

new_quiz.q: What do you send as proof for the input part of this quest?
choices: A written description of the chain from input to movement
A video of the character jumping
A copy of the character Blueprint file
A screenshot of the Content Browser
new_quiz.explain: You describe in 4 to 6 lines how one input travels from the key press to the movement. Writing it down shows that you understood each step.

new_quiz.q: What is a test harness level?
choices: The first level of your finished game
A level that holds every asset of the project
A small, empty level that you build only for testing
A level that Unreal creates when a test fails
new_quiz.explain: A test harness has nothing in it except the things you want to test. It exists to make testing simple.

new_quiz.q: Why is a bug easier to understand in a level that is almost empty?
choices: Empty levels have no collision
Empty levels cannot have bugs
Empty levels are saved more often
Nothing else in the level can cause or hide the problem
new_quiz.explain: With only the tested things in the level, there are few possible causes. The bug is easier to repeat and to understand.

new_quiz.q: What is a pad in the test harness?
choices: A marked area on the floor for one system you plan to test
A Blueprint that runs all tests in a row
A window that shows test results
A note that is saved with the level
new_quiz.explain: Each pad is a marked area for one system, for example one for a pickup and one for a door. This keeps the tests apart.

new_quiz.q: How do you show what each pad is for?
choices: Give each pad a different sound
Add a Text Render actor next to it with the name of the pad
Write the name in the World Settings
Place a Player Start on each pad
new_quiz.explain: A Text Render actor shows text in the level. With the name of the pad as its text, anyone can read what the pad tests.

new_quiz.q: Simulate runs the level without a player. How do you trigger the interactable on a pad in Simulate?
choices: Press the E key in the viewport
Walk the character onto the pad
Drop a physics cube onto the pad
Type the name of the pad in the console
new_quiz.explain: There is no character in Simulate, so something else must overlap the pad. A physics cube that falls onto it does the job.

new_quiz.q: Why do you set the GameMode Override of the level in the World Settings panel?
choices: So the level loads faster
So the level always starts with the same GameMode
So the level cannot be edited by others
So the level has no Player Start
new_quiz.explain: With the override set, the level does not depend on the project default. It always starts the same way, which makes tests repeatable.

new_quiz.q: What is a debug room?
choices: A test level where each area shows one way to find problems
A window that lists all errors of the project
A folder where crash files are saved
A level that players see when the game crashes
new_quiz.explain: A debug room is a test level with several pads. Each pad shows one debug technique.

new_quiz.q: How do you make a Print String node write to the Output Log only?
choices: Set its duration to 0
Give it an empty Key
Set its color to black
Turn off Print to Screen on the node
new_quiz.explain: Print String can write to the screen and to the log. With Print to Screen turned off, the message only appears in the Output Log.

new_quiz.q: What does it mean to reproduce a test?
choices: To copy the test level to a new project
To follow the steps and run the test again
To delete the test and write a new one
To record the test as a video
new_quiz.explain: To reproduce is to run the same steps again and get the same result. Your notes must give those steps.

new_quiz.q: Besides the steps to reproduce, what do your notes for each test say?
choices: How long you worked on the pad
Which mesh the pad uses
What output you expect to see
Who built the pad
new_quiz.explain: The expected output tells the reader what a correct run looks like. Without it, nobody can tell if the test passed.

new_quiz.q: One pad has a Blueprint that is ready for a breakpoint. What is a breakpoint?
choices: A mark that pauses the game on a node you choose
A place where the level ends
A message in the Output Log
A pad that breaks when you step on it
new_quiz.explain: A breakpoint pauses the game when the marked node runs. You can then look at the values in the graph.

new_quiz.q: Which console command do you run in the room to write down timing numbers?
choices: stat none
show collision
stat unit
print string
new_quiz.explain: The command stat unit shows timing numbers on the screen. You note them and add one line that says what they mean.

new_quiz.q: Where do you choose how Play In Editor (PIE) opens?
choices: In the Output Log, under Filters
In the three dots menu next to the Play button in the main toolbar
In the World Settings, under GameMode
In the Content Browser, under Settings
new_quiz.explain: The three dots next to the Play button open the play options. There you pick New Editor Window (PIE) or Selected Viewport.

new_quiz.q: What does the play option Selected Viewport do?
choices: It records the viewport to a video
It opens the game on a second computer
It opens the game in a new window
It runs the game inside the level viewport
new_quiz.explain: Selected Viewport plays the game in the viewport you already have. New Editor Window (PIE) opens a separate window for the game.

new_quiz.q: Where do you find the setting Show Frame Rate and Memory?
choices: In Edit, then Editor Preferences, under General, then Performance
In Edit, then Plugins, under Performance
In Window, then Output Log
In the Show menu of the viewport
new_quiz.explain: The setting is an editor preference. You open Edit, then Editor Preferences, and go to General, then Performance.

new_quiz.q: What changes when you turn on Show Frame Rate and Memory?
choices: The game runs at a fixed frame rate
The editor uses less memory
The editor shows these numbers at all times
The numbers are written to a file
new_quiz.explain: The frame rate and memory use stay visible in the editor. You notice at once when a change makes the editor slower.

new_quiz.q: What is the Source Code Editor setting in the Editor Preferences?
choices: The folder where Blueprints are saved
The language of the editor menus
The font of the Blueprint graphs
The program that Unreal opens when you read or write C++ code
new_quiz.explain: This setting names the program for C++ code. You find it under General, then Source Code.

new_quiz.q: When should you change the Source Code Editor setting?
choices: Only if you use a different program for your code
Every time you create a new project
Before every Play In Editor session
Only if the frame rate is low
new_quiz.explain: The setting should match the program you really use. If it is already right, you only note what it is set to.

new_quiz.q: What is Unreal Insights?
choices: A panel that lists the assets of the project
A window that shows Blueprint errors
A plugin that makes the game run faster
A profiling tool that records where the engine spends its time
new_quiz.explain: Unreal Insights is a profiling tool. It records the work of the engine so that you can see which part takes long.

new_quiz.q: What is a trace?
choices: A line drawn in the viewport
A recording made for Unreal Insights
A list of keyboard shortcuts
A copy of the level
new_quiz.explain: A recording of what the engine did is called a trace. You open it in Unreal Insights to study it.

new_quiz.q: How do you start a trace from the editor?
choices: Click Trace in the bar at the bottom of the editor window and choose Start Trace
Open Edit, then Plugins, and choose Start Trace
Right-click the level in the Content Browser and choose Start Trace
Open the Show menu of the viewport and choose Start Trace
new_quiz.explain: The Trace menu is in the bar at the bottom of the editor window. The same menu has Stop Trace and the entry that opens Unreal Insights.

new_quiz.q: What does the Game thread do?
choices: It saves the project to disk
It prepares what is drawn
It runs the game logic
It plays the sounds of the editor
new_quiz.explain: A thread is one line of work that the engine runs. The Game thread runs the game logic, such as Blueprints and movement.

new_quiz.q: What does the Render thread do?
choices: It runs the game logic
It prepares what is drawn
It reads the keyboard input
It records the trace
new_quiz.explain: The Render thread prepares the things that are drawn on the screen. In a trace you find it next to the Game thread.

new_quiz.q: A game runs slowly. What can a trace tell you?
choices: Which key the player pressed last
Which asset has the longest name
Which level was saved last
Which part of the work takes too long
new_quiz.explain: The timing view shows how long each part of a frame takes. The part that takes too long is where you start to look for the cause.

new_quiz.q: Where do you look up and change the shortcuts of the editor?
choices: In Window, then Output Log
In Edit, then Plugins
In Edit, then Editor Preferences, under Keyboard Shortcuts
In the World Settings panel
new_quiz.explain: The Keyboard Shortcuts section of the Editor Preferences lists every command with its key. You can search it and change any shortcut.

new_quiz.q: What does it mean to rebind a command?
choices: To give the command a new key
To remove the command from the editor
To run the command two times
To move the command to another menu
new_quiz.explain: Rebinding gives a command a new key. The command itself stays the same.

new_quiz.q: How do you set a new shortcut for a command in the Keyboard Shortcuts section?
choices: Type the name of the key in the console
Click the text field of the command and press the key combination
Drag the command onto the main toolbar
Right-click the command and choose Rename
new_quiz.explain: You click the text field next to the command and press the keys you want. The shortcut is saved when you click outside the field.

new_quiz.q: You press a key combination that another command already uses. What happens?
choices: The editor closes without saving
Both commands are deleted
The key is silently given to both commands
A warning appears, and you can click Override to replace the old binding
new_quiz.explain: The editor warns you about the conflict. Override gives the key to the new command, and clicking outside the field keeps the old binding.

new_quiz.q: How can you take your custom shortcuts to another installation of Unreal Engine?
choices: Copy the project folder
Use the Export button, which saves them as an .ini file
Take a screenshot of the list
Restart the editor two times
new_quiz.explain: The Export button saves your shortcuts as an .ini file. On the other installation, the Import button loads that file.

new_quiz.q: Why is it worth binding shortcuts for the commands you use while testing?
choices: Shortcuts make the game run faster
Shortcuts are needed before a Blueprint can compile
You run the same few commands many times, so each shortcut saves many clicks
Commands without a shortcut stop working after a while
new_quiz.explain: Testing repeats the same actions again and again. One key for each of them saves a little time on every run, and that adds up.
